newsitem.title: UK: FTSE's fate hangs on monetary meetings next week.
newsitem.headline: FTSE's fate hangs on monetary meetings next week.

text.p: The fate of London's share market hangs on monetary meetings in the U.S. and UK next week which could put the upward drive in the FTSE 100 index back on course or stop the bull run dead in its tracks.
The spectre of a sharp sell-off sparked by a U.S. rate rise will keep markets spooked ahead of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on Tuesday and Wednesday, analysts say.
February 4 is the three-year anniversary of an unexpected U.S interest rate rise which sent world stock markets reeling. Some analysts believe history could repeat itself.
"Memories of February 1994 will play large in investors' minds, especially given the great January we've had," said David Aserkoff, a strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston.
"But given the relatively positive Employment Cost Index data we saw recently, I think a rate hike at the FOMC is less than likely."
Robert Buckland, UK equity strategist at HSBC James Capel, said the market was divided over whether rates would rise.
"It's a fateful anniversary," he said. "On balance we're not expecting a rate rise but it's definitely quite a close call. It will be the key focus of all world markets next week"

Nerves will be further frayed by the UK's monthly monetary meeting on Wednesday between Chancellor Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England governor Eddie George. The minutes of the December meeting showed George pressing for a half-point rate rise.
"I don't expect a UK rate rise," Buckland said. "You can guess right now what will happen -- Eddie George is going to call for higher rates and the chancellor is probably going to turn him down."
But some said a modest tightening of interest rates could not be ruled out. "It's unlikely we'll see a half point rise, the debate is between a quarter and no change," one trader said.

"Short sterling is telling you that a rise of a quarter of a percentage point is expected by March, and one or two people maybe expect a bit more," he said. "There's going to be increasing nervousness ahead of the meeting."
Dealers said a rate hike in either country would pull the FTSE back from its recent highs, but the biggest risk was from a U.S. rate rise which halts the bull run on Wall Street.

"If there is a U.S. rate hike next week it's certainly going to be tough in the short run," Buckland said. "We wouldn't expect to see as dramatic a sell-off as we saw in 1994 but it would be a cause for concern, there's no doubt about that."

Aserkoff said that if U.S. rates stayed down, markets would be boosted by "decent relief trade". "If the Fed does raise rates, people will start to wonder whether it was a one-off or whether more are on the way," he said.

Although monetary meetings will dominate the week, several important data releases are also due. Monday sees the release of the UK January Purchasing Managers Index and M0, as well as the North American Purchasing Managers (NAPM) index in the U.S. And on Friday, U.S. January non-farm payrolls are due. The week also sees the start of the seasonal flood of company results.
Airports company BAA Plc reports third-quarter results on Monday and broadcaster BSKyB announces its half-year figures on Wednesday.
On Thursday, British Telecom releases third-quarter figures and ICI reports its annual results.
On Friday, retailer Safeway publishes its Christmas trading statement.

Speculation about the date of Britain's general election, which must be held by May 22, would also keep the market on its toes next week, dealers said. "There are rumours flying all over the place," one said. "Maybe next week we'll find out."
